opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I'd start with the basic problem: if you're on the outside trying to figure out whether an AI company is actually being careful, you mostly have to rely on what the company tells you. And companies have pretty strong incentives to present themselves favorably. That's not necessarily bad faith. Often the people writing the safety documentation sincerely believe things are going well. But self-assessment has well-known failure modes. You tend to test for the things you already thought of, you interpret ambiguous results charitably, and when there's commercial pressure to ship, the bar for "good enough" can quietly drift.

Third-party evaluations help with a few of those problems at once.

The first is independence. An external evaluator doesn't have a launch date riding on the outcome, so they're more willing to report something uncomfortable and less likely to explain it away.

The second is fresh eyes. People inside a lab develop shared assumptions about what the model can and can't do and which risks matter. An outside group with different expertise, say people who've spent years on cybersecurity or biosecurity, will often probe in directions the internal team simply didn't think to try. Capability elicitation is genuinely hard. Whether you find a dangerous capability depends a lot on how hard and how cleverly you push, so having more diverse people pushing is valuable.

The third is comparability. If the same evaluator, or the same standardized methodology, is applied across multiple developers, you can say something meaningful about how companies compare. Otherwise every lab reports results on its own slightly different setup and it's very hard to draw conclusions.

And the fourth is that it builds infrastructure for the future. Even if today's evaluations are imperfect, establishing the norm that models get externally tested before deployment, and building organizations with the skills and access to do that well, puts us in a much better position as systems get more capable and the stakes go up. It's much easier to strengthen an existing practice than to invent one in a hurry during a crisis.

That said, I'd add some caveats. Third-party evaluations are only as good as the access the evaluators get. If they get a few days with a model shortly before launch, without the ability to fine-tune it or see the relevant internal context, there's a real limit to what they can find. There's also a risk of "safety-washing," where a company can say "we were externally evaluated" and that becomes a box-ticking exercise rather than a real check. So I see them as one of the best tools we have, not a complete answer. They work best alongside good internal practices, transparency about methodology, and ideally some mechanism by which the results actually feed into deployment decisions.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations depend on access, expertise, and how thoroughly evaluators probe, but does not state that choosing appropriate evaluations requires detailed knowledge of the circumstances.

r002.rationale: It describes external evaluators bringing fresh perspectives and different expertise, but does not identify accumulated deep contextual knowledge as the basis for nuanced judgments.

r003.rationale: It says external evaluators lack a launch date tied to the outcome and are less likely to explain away uncomfortable findings, while noting insiders’ shared assumptions and commercial pressures.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose safety scorecards as a stepping stone when political conditions hinder third-party evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic problem is that from the outside, it's really hard to tell what a company is actually doing on safety. You see the blog posts, you see the policy documents, you see people saying nice things in interviews — but all of that is cheap. Any company can write a responsible scaling policy. The question is whether the thing they wrote down bears any relationship to what's happening when a model is about to ship and there's a lot of commercial pressure to get it out the door.

And the people who do know the answer to that are inside the company, and they have obvious incentives — not even necessarily bad-faith ones, just the normal thing where you're close to the work and you believe in it and you tend to give yourself the benefit of the doubt. I include myself in that. I think DeepMind takes safety seriously, but I would say that, right? I'm not the person you should be asking.

So what third-party evaluations give you is someone who isn't on the payroll, who can actually look at the model, run their own tests, and say "here's what we found." That does a few things at once. It gives the public and policymakers a signal that isn't just the company's word. It creates an incentive for the company to not have embarrassing gaps, because someone external might catch them. And honestly, it's useful internally too — evaluators sometimes find things the internal teams missed, because they're coming at it with fresh eyes and different assumptions.

I'd also say it's one of the more tractable interventions. A lot of proposals for improving company safety practices require either regulation that doesn't exist yet or a level of trust in the company that isn't warranted. Third-party evals don't need either of those. You need some competent evaluators, you need the companies to give them access, and you need the results to be shared in some form. All of those are hard, but they're the kind of hard where you can see what progress looks like.

Now, I don't want to oversell it. The current ecosystem is pretty immature. Evaluators often get limited access, limited time, they're testing a model that's basically already decided to ship. And evaluations can only find what they're looking for — if the dangerous capability is something nobody thought to test, an eval won't save you. So I think of it as necessary but definitely not sufficient. It's the piece of the puzzle that makes the other pieces checkable, which is why I rate it so highly, but it's not a substitute for the companies actually having good internal practices.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluators need access and can miss risks they did not think to test, but does not state that choosing suitable evaluations requires detailed knowledge of the circumstances.

r002.rationale: It says external evaluators can inspect models and bring fresh eyes, but does not identify accumulated deep contextual knowledge as the basis for nuanced judgments.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts outside evaluators with insiders, who have incentives and may give themselves the benefit of the doubt.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose safety scorecards as a stepping stone or discuss political conditions hindering third-party evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic problem is that it’s quite hard to tell from the outside whether a company’s safety practices are actually good. You can look at the policies they publish, but there’s a big gap between having a policy that sounds sensible and implementing it well. And the company saying, “We think we’re doing a good job,” is clearly not enough on its own.

Third-party evaluations can give you an independent source of evidence. Ideally, you have technically competent people who get enough access to examine what the company is actually doing: what it tests for, whether those tests are informative, and what happens when they find a problem. Does that result change a deployment decision, or does it just end up in a report?

There are limitations, of course. An evaluator might not get the access they need, or their tests might miss important risks. So I wouldn’t treat an evaluation as a stamp that says, “This company is safe.” But I do think it can make the company’s claims much more checkable. That’s a substantial improvement over asking everyone to take those claims on trust.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluators should examine the company’s tests and responses to problems, but does not state that choosing appropriate evaluations requires detailed knowledge of the circumstances.

r002.rationale: It calls for technically competent evaluators with enough access to inspect practices, but does not identify accumulated deep contextual knowledge as the basis for nuanced judgments.

r003.rationale: The response contrasts independent evidence with companies’ own claims, but does not say third-party evaluators are less subject to internal company biases.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention safety scorecards or present them as a stepping stone when political conditions hinder third-party evaluations.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic problem is that, from the outside, it’s very hard to tell how seriously a company is taking safety. You can read its policies, you can look at what its leaders say, but those are relatively cheap signals. You’d really like to know: when there’s a conflict between shipping something and addressing a safety concern, what actually happens?

An independent evaluator can potentially get access to evidence that the public doesn’t have—results of internal tests, details of the safeguards, how decisions were made—and assess whether the company’s claims are justified. And if the evaluator uses a reasonably consistent standard across companies, that makes comparisons much more meaningful.

Of course, that only works if the evaluation is substantive. If the company picks a friendly evaluator, restricts what they can see, and controls what gets published, you haven’t learned very much. So I’d want to know how independent the evaluator is, what access they had, and what their conclusions actually cover.

I wouldn’t treat a positive evaluation as a guarantee of safety. But it can give us a much stronger basis for judging a company’s practices than just trusting its public commitments.

r001.rationale: It discusses evaluator access to internal evidence and decision-making, but does not say that selecting appropriate evaluations requires detailed knowledge of the circumstances.

r002.rationale: It says evaluators can access internal tests, safeguards, and decision-making details to assess whether safety claims are justified, supporting more informed judgments.

r003.rationale: It asks whether evaluators are independent, but does not identify them as less subject to bias than people inside AI companies.

r004.rationale: It does not propose safety scorecards as a stepping stone or discuss political barriers to third-party evaluations.
